newsitem.title: USA: Ivory Coast says debt relief will help reform.
newsitem.headline: Ivory Coast says debt relief will help reform.

text.p: A decision paving the way for improved debt relief for the Ivory Coast will make it easier to press ahead with economic reforms, Finance Minister N'Goran Niamien said on Tuesday.
He told Reuters that the Ivory Coast expected to hold talks with the International Monetary Fund next month on a new three-year program of IMF-backed economic reforms.
"We are not asking for a blank check. The fact that we have been given access to this (new debt relief) will help us continue our economic reforms," he said.

The IMF agreed last week to widen guidelines on which countries qualify to benefit from a new debt relief initiative being carried out jointly with the World Bank and Paris Club of creditor nations to help poor heavily-indebted nations.
Around 15 to 20 countries, mostly in Africa, are expected to benefit.

France, which had pledged to help Ivory Coast, its senior ally in West Africa, had pushed for a widening of the guidelines to allow countries with comparatively healthy exports to benefit. The Ivory Coast would otherwise have been excluded.
The Ivorian Finance Minister said he could not say right now how much money would be involved in the new debt relief, but said he hoped it would come through as quickly as possible.
Under the initiative, the Paris Club of creditor nations can write off up to 80 percent of debt due during a period covered by an IMF-backed economic reform program.
The IMF and World Bank will also take action at the same time to reduce money owed to them.
The IMF and World Bank last week approved plans for Uganda to get the debt relief, making it the first to benefit from the debt relief initiative.

But the institutions disappointed developing countries by setting April 1998 as the starting point when the debt relief will kick in, raising worries that other countries that follow Uganda will not see the benefits until even later.

Niamien said Ivory Coast wanted the debt relief as quickly as possible. He said he hoped it might not have as long a wait as Uganda between approval by the IMF and World Bank and the start of the debt relief.
The IMF and World Bank boards are expected to approve Ivory Coast's right to debt relief shortly.
"We don't know, whether there will indeed be an interim period," Niamien said.
The decision to set April 1998 as the start date for Uganda is meant to leave time to monitor Uganda's progress in implementing economic reforms.
